guided.title: Countries of employees and suppliers
guided.prompt: Return one column `country` with every distinct country where there is at least one employee or at least one supplier, in alphabetical order. Use `UNION` of the `country` columns of `employees` and `suppliers`.
guided.solution:
SELECT country FROM employees
UNION
SELECT country FROM suppliers
ORDER BY country;
hints: The starter only reads one table, and it repeats countries. A set operator combines two queries.
UNION returns the rows of both queries and removes duplicates. ORDER BY goes at the very end.
SELECT country FROM employees UNION SELECT country FROM suppliers ORDER BY country

guided.title: German customers and suppliers in one list
guided.prompt: Stack the customers and the suppliers located in Germany into one list with the columns `kind` (the text `customer` or `supplier`), `name` (the `company_name`) and `city`. Keep all rows (use `UNION ALL`) and order by `kind`, then `name`.
guided.starter:
-- Customers and suppliers in Germany, with a kind label
SELECT 'customer' AS kind, company_name AS name, city
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'Germany'
ORDER BY kind, name;
guided.solution:
SELECT 'customer' AS kind, company_name AS name, city
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'Germany'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'supplier', company_name, city
FROM suppliers
WHERE country = 'Germany'
ORDER BY kind, name;
hints: The starter has only the customer part. Add the supplier part as a second query.
Join the two queries with UNION ALL. The second query needs the same three columns in the same order.
SELECT 'supplier', company_name, city FROM suppliers WHERE country = 'Germany'

guided.title: Countries with customers and suppliers
guided.prompt: Return one column `country` listing the countries that have at least one customer and at least one supplier. Use `INTERSECT`. Order by `country`.
guided.solution:
SELECT country FROM customers
INTERSECT
SELECT country FROM suppliers
ORDER BY country;
hints: The starter lists customer countries with repeats. You need the countries that are also in the suppliers table.
INTERSECT returns the distinct rows that appear in both queries.
SELECT country FROM customers INTERSECT SELECT country FROM suppliers ORDER BY country

guided.title: Products never ordered, with EXCEPT
guided.prompt: Return `product_id` for every product that does not appear in `order_details`, using `EXCEPT` between the `product_id` columns of `products` and `order_details`. Order by `product_id`.
guided.solution:
SELECT product_id FROM products
EXCEPT
SELECT product_id FROM order_details
ORDER BY product_id;
hints: The starter returns all products. Subtract the ordered ones.
EXCEPT returns the rows of the first query that are not in the second. The order of the two queries matters.
SELECT product_id FROM products EXCEPT SELECT product_id FROM order_details ORDER BY product_id

independent.title: A UK directory of three kinds of contacts
independent.prompt: Build one list of contacts located in the UK from three tables, with the columns `kind`, `contact_name`, `company` and `country`, in that order. For customers and suppliers use the label `customer` or `supplier`, `contact_name` and `company_name`. For employees use the label `employee`, the full name `first_name || ' ' || last_name` as `contact_name` and the constant text `Northwind staff` as `company`. Keep every row (`UNION ALL`) and order by `kind`, then `contact_name`.
independent.starter:
-- UK contacts from customers, suppliers and employees
SELECT 'customer' AS kind, contact_name, company_name AS company, country
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'UK'
ORDER BY kind, contact_name;
independent.solution:
SELECT 'customer' AS kind, contact_name, company_name AS company, country
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'UK'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'supplier', contact_name, company_name, country
FROM suppliers
WHERE country = 'UK'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'employee', first_name || ' ' || last_name, 'Northwind staff', country
FROM employees
WHERE country = 'UK'
ORDER BY kind, contact_name;

independent.title: Customers active in 1996 and 1998 but not in 1997
independent.prompt: Find the customers who placed at least one order in 1996 and at least one in 1998 but none in 1997. Combine three queries on `orders` that return `customer_id` with `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` (years by `order_date` ranges, for example from 1996-01-01 up to but not including 1997-01-01). Use the result as a list in `customers` so the final output has `customer_id` and `company_name`, ordered by `customer_id`.
independent.starter:
-- Customers with orders in 1996 and 1998 but not in 1997
SELECT customer_id, company_name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date < '1997-01-01')
ORDER BY customer_id;
independent.solution:
SELECT customer_id, company_name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= '1996-01-01' AND order_date < '1997-01-01'
  INTERSECT
  SELECT customer_id FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= '1998-01-01' AND order_date < '1999-01-01'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT customer_id FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= '1997-01-01' AND order_date < '1998-01-01'
)
ORDER BY customer_id;

independent.title: Which countries host several kinds of contacts?
independent.prompt: Stretch task. Stack the `country` of every customer (label `customer`), supplier (`supplier`) and employee (`employee`) with `UNION ALL` into a CTE `entities(kind, country)`. Then return, per `country`, the columns `customers`, `suppliers` and `employees` (the number of rows of each kind, use `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = ...)`), keeping only countries that have at least 2 different kinds. Order by `country`.
independent.starter:
-- Contact counts per country and kind (countries with 2+ kinds)
SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS customers, 0 AS suppliers, 0 AS employees
FROM customers
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY country;
independent.solution:
WITH entities AS (
  SELECT 'customer' AS kind, country FROM customers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'supplier', country FROM suppliers
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'employee', country FROM employees
)
SELECT country,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'customer') AS customers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'supplier') AS suppliers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'employee') AS employees
FROM entities
GROUP BY country
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT kind) >= 2
ORDER BY country;

checks.question: `customers` has 91 rows and `suppliers` has 29. How many rows does `SELECT country FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT country FROM suppliers` return?
checks.explanation: UNION ALL keeps every row of both queries, so 91 + 29 = 120. Plain UNION would remove duplicates and return only the 25 different countries.

checks.question: Which statement about `A EXCEPT B` and `B EXCEPT A` is true?
options: They always return the same rows
They can differ, because EXCEPT returns what is in the first query and not in the second
Only one of them is allowed in PostgreSQL
Both return the rows common to A and B
checks.explanation: EXCEPT is not symmetric. Customers' countries except suppliers' countries gives 9 rows, whereas suppliers' countries except customers' countries gives 4 rows.

checks.question: What happens with `SELECT company_name FROM customers UNION SELECT 1`?
options: It returns the names and a row with 1
It fails with 'UNION types character varying and integer cannot be matched'
It converts all values to numbers
It returns only the row with 1
checks.explanation: Columns in the same position must have compatible types. Text and integer are not compatible without an explicit cast. SELECT 1::text, or selecting a text constant, would work.

checks.question: Both `customers.region` and `suppliers.region` are NULL in every row. How many rows does `SELECT region FROM customers UNION SELECT region FROM suppliers` return?
options: 0, because NULL never equals NULL
1, because set operators treat NULLs as equal
120, because NULLs are never removed
An error
checks.explanation: For duplicate removal, set operators treat two NULLs as the same value, unlike an = comparison in WHERE. So all the NULL rows collapse into one.

checks.question: Where does `ORDER BY` belong in `SELECT a FROM t1 UNION SELECT a FROM t2`?
options: After the first query, so that it sorts only t1
After the last query, where it sorts the whole combined result
In both queries, otherwise it is ignored
It cannot be used with UNION
checks.explanation: ORDER BY (and LIMIT) apply to the combined result and are written once at the end. To sort only one part you must wrap that query in parentheses.

checks.question: What does `SELECT x FROM a UNION SELECT y FROM b INTERSECT SELECT z FROM c` compute, without parentheses?
options: (a UNION b) INTERSECT c
a UNION (b INTERSECT c)
Left to right, one operator after another
An error
checks.explanation: INTERSECT binds more tightly than UNION and EXCEPT, in the same way that AND binds before OR. Write parentheses to state your intention explicitly.
